######################################
2. Define Functions
#######################################
Functions
```{r}
f_biplot <- function(load,pc){
  plot_dat <- as.data.frame(load[,pc])
  plot_dat$labels <- row.names(plot_dat)
  plot_dat$start_x <- 0
  plot_dat$stary_y <- 0
  max_lim <- ceiling(max(abs(plot_dat[,1:2])))
  
  p <- ggplot(plot_dat) + 
    geom_segment(aes(x=plot_dat$start_x,y=plot_dat$stary_y,xend=plot_dat[,1],yend=plot_dat[,2]),arrow = arrow(length=unit(0.2,'cm'))) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-max_lim,max_lim),ylim=c(-max_lim,max_lim)) + xlab(names(plot_dat)[1]) + ylab(names(plot_dat)[2]) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_text_repel(mapping = aes(label=plot_dat$labels,x=plot_dat[,1],y=plot_dat[,2]))
  plot(p)
}

f_screeplot <- function(pca_res){
  prop <- (pca_res$sdev)^2/sum((pca_res$sdev)^2)
  cum_prop <- cumsum(prop)
  cum_prop_label <- paste0(round(100*cum_prop,2),'%')
  plot_dat <- data.frame(PC=paste0('PC',1:length(cum_prop)), sd=pca_res$sdev,prop=prop,cum_prop=cum_prop,label=cum_prop_label)

  p <- ggplot(plot_dat,aes(x=reorder(PC,cum_prop),y=sd)) + geom_bar(stat="identity") + theme_bw() +
       xlab('PC') + geom_text(aes(label = label),vjust=-1)
  plot(p)
}

f_loadings <- function(pca_res){
  plot_dat <- as.data.frame(pca_res$rotation^2)
  plot_dat$vul <- row.names(plot_dat)
  plot_dat <- plot_dat %>% gather(PC, wt, -vul)
  plot_dat$wt <- round(100*plot_dat$wt,2)
  plot_dat$order <- as.numeric(sub('.*PC', '', plot_dat$PC))
  
  p <- ggplot(data = plot_dat, aes(fill = vul, y = wt, x = reorder(PC, order))) +
    geom_bar(position = "stack", stat = "identity") +
    ylab('Contribution Wt') + xlab('PC')
  
  plot(p)
}

f_loadings_1 <- function(pca_res,start_pc, end_pc){
  plot_dat <- as.data.frame(pca_res$rotation^2)
  plot_dat$vul <- row.names(plot_dat)
  plot_dat <- plot_dat %>% gather(PC, wt, -vul)
  plot_dat$wt <- round(100*plot_dat$wt,2)
  plot_dat$order <- as.numeric(sub('.*PC', '', plot_dat$PC))
  
  plot_dat <- plot_dat %>%
    filter(order >= start_pc & order <= end_pc)
  
  p <- ggplot(data = plot_dat, aes(fill = vul, y = wt, x = reorder(PC, order))) +
    geom_bar(position = "stack", stat = "identity") +
    ylab('Contribution Wt') + xlab('PC')
  
  plot(p)
}

f_eigenvalues <- function(pca_res){
  eigenvalues <- pca_res$sdev^2
  plot_data <- data.frame(PC = paste0('PC', 1:length(eigenvalues)), Eigenvalues = eigenvalues)

  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = reorder(PC, -Eigenvalues), y = Eigenvalues)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "#2A3B90") +  
    geom_text(aes(label = round(Eigenvalues, 2)), vjust = -1) +  
    geom_line(aes(x = reorder(PC, -Eigenvalues), y = Eigenvalues), color = "#92278F", group = 1) +
    theme_bw() +
    xlab('PC') +
    ylab('Eigenvalues') +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))  # Rotating x-axis labels for readability

  plot(p)
}
```

Note before PCA
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# By treating categorical variables as a series of dummy variables (one-hot encoding), each category becomes a separate binary variable, therefore, we should look to see if any one of the categories (of the original categorical variable) provides unique information that is not captured by the other categories (e.g., explains variations in the data that the other categories do not). If one 'level' of the cateogry explains something the others don't in at least on PC dimension then should include it.

# First, decide the number of PCs or dimensions to retain (elbow, cumulative explained variances)
# Select variables: (1) on the biplot, those grouping or overlapping with each other indicates strong positive correlation with each other, 90 degree => uncorrelated; help us to drop correlated variables (2) among the correlated variables, if a var stands out showing stronger association with the retained PCs, use this var and drop others who correlated with it

# About variables having categories with (relatively) small size: although categories with low frequencies leave limited distributional information in that space for model fit, small categories may be informative in some cases. In addition, it'd be better to look at the the number of observations instead of the percentage of the total sample given that we are working with an enormously large sample size. Therefore, at this stage, we will not drop variables based on small % of the sample alone, unless we are deciding between two variables of the same underlying measure with similarly strong factor loadings. We'll have another step after the initial LCA where we can prune and remove variables that don't show much variability across the segments. 
```

## 1. Domain 1: Woman and her past experiences
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Decision made after 1st and 2nd round: () marr/cohab and pship.cat are highly correlated. Chose marr/cohab, drop pship.cat. (2) keep ed.lev.cat1 (3) a few age related measures are highly correlated, use early.cohab.19 and drop the other age related measures.
# The tricky one is the media exposure measures. The biplots in "media specific" show the positively correlation between freq.rad and freq.newsp and media.sum.2plus, while freq.tv and freq.net often show diffrent directions than media.sum.2plus. Considering their associations with the retained PCs, we are trying (1) drop the individual media sources and bring media.sum.2plus for PCA with other measures (2) drop media.sum.2plus and bring individual ones. Then compare.
```

```{r}
domain1.var <- const[const$category=='Woman and her past experiences' & !is.na(const$category),'f.var.name']
# Check whether all variables in this domain have the correct data type for the type of variable they represent. PCA is applicable to numerical data only as it is based on linear algebra calculations. For binary coded as numeric (0, 1), PCA can handle it without issues. For binary or categorical variables, 'character' is okay. For numeric, continuous, or ordinal variables, the data type should be 'numeric' or 'integer' if they are represented as numerical values. In the case of IND DHS, from script 4, the numeric variables in this domain are all binary.

(2) Social mnental models -> Internalized gender norms -> Early marriage. Therefore, here it generated the "second" one "early.cohab.19.1". ### 1.0. Correlation matrix 
```{r,echo=TRUE}
# using the cor(), correlation coefficient is not calculated in corr.matrix.d1 below for some variables given the small size of certain categories. Note that cor() applies to numeric variables only.
```

```{r}
d1.data <- dhs.seg[,..domain1.var]

summary_table <- data.frame(Variable = character(0), Category = character(0), Frequency = integer(0), Percentage = numeric(0))

for (variable_name in names(d1.data)) {
  freq_table <- table(d1.data[[variable_name]])
  freq_df <- data.frame(Variable = variable_name, Category = names(freq_table), Frequency = as.numeric(freq_table))
  
  total_samples <- sum(!is.na(d1.data[[variable_name]]))
  freq_df$Percentage <- freq_df$Frequency / total_samples
  
  summary_table <- rbind(summary_table, freq_df)
}
summary_table
```

  for (j in (i + 1):length(d2c2.var)) {

    chi_square_test <- chisq.test(cross_tab)

    # Store the results in the data frame
    result <- data.frame(
      Variables = paste(var1, "vs", var2),
      ChiSquare = chi_square_test$statistic,
      DegreesOfFreedom = chi_square_test$parameter,
      PValue = chi_square_test$p.value
    )
    
    correlation_results <- rbind(correlation_results, result)
  }
}

print(correlation_results)

domain3.var <- const[const$category=='Household economics and living conditions' & !is.na(const$category),'f.var.name']

domain3.var <- domain3.var[!domain3.var %in% d3c1.drop]
#lapply(dhs.seg[,..domain3.var],class)

domain4.var <- const[const$category=='Health mental models' & !is.na(const$category),'f.var.name']

names(dhs.seg[,..domain4.var])

```

### 4.1. Summary
```{r}
summary(d4)
```

### 4.2. Screeplot
#### 4.2.1. Eigenvalues
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# "elbow" at PC3
```

```{r,fig.height= 8}
f_eigenvalues(d4)
```

#### 4.2.2. Explained variances per PC
```{r}
fviz_eig(d4, addlabels = TRUE, ylim = c(0, 35), linecolor = "#92278F") 
```

#### 4.2.3. Cumulative explained variances
```{r, fig.height= 12, fig.width=12, echo=TRUE}
#Look at screeplot to determine how many PC's capture the variation in the data, first applying rule of thumb around 60%
f_screeplot(d4)

# SD measures the variability of data points along a PC. A higher SD indicates that the PC captures more variability in the data.
# PC1 explains 25% of the total variances, PC2 explains 21%, and PC3 explains another 14%. Retaining PC1, PC2, PC3 will give a cumulative explained variance of 60.17%.
```

### 4.3. Examine the loadings
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# PC1 primarily captures information related med.distance. The other perceived barriers to healthcare (med.cost, med.permis, med.alone) also show moderate positive association. med.distance and med.cost are correlated (tested earlier). 
# PC2 primarily captures information related to auto.contra (full or partial autonomy on deciding contraceptives). 
# PC 3 primarily captures information related to auto.contra (no control over)
```

```{r}
d4$rotation
f_loadings(pca_res = d4)
```

### 4.4. Examine biplots
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Although auto.contra contributes little to PC1, it shows high association with PC2 and PC3 (and PC1 alone explains only 25% of the total variances. Propose to use auto.contra.
# The med.xxx (perceived berries to healthcare) show moderate to high positive associations with PC1, while little influence in PC2 or PC3. Note that med.permis and med.cost are also mapped to other domains. Check how they perform there. 
```

```{r}
f_biplot(d4$rotation,pc=c(1,2))   #PCA 1/2
f_biplot(d4$rotation,pc=c(1,3))   #PCA 1/3
f_biplot(d4$rotation,pc=c(2,3))   #PCA 2/3
```
